p.x:
Last month my family moved to a new flat in Chiang Mai. It is on the fourth floor of a building near the old city. There are three bedrooms, a living room, a small kitchen and a bathroom. My bedroom has a big window, and I can see the mountains from my bed!
When we arrived, the flat had no furniture. We bought a new sofa, a table and four chairs for the living room, and a wardrobe for my clothes. The sofa is very comfortable, and my cat sleeps on it all day.
The best thing is the garden. It's downstairs, and everyone in the building can use it. My little brother plays there every afternoon. The only problem is the lift. It's often broken, so we have to carry our shopping upstairs. Last week my father forgot his key, and we waited outside the door for an hour!

Renting your first flat is exciting, but there are a few things you should know before you sign anything. First, visit the neighbourhood at different times of day. A street that seems quiet at 10 a.m. might be very noisy at night. Ask other tenants what they think of the landlord. Does he repair things quickly?
Second, check the flat carefully. Look for signs of a leak on the ceiling, test the taps and the air conditioner, and make sure the windows lock. A flat may look spacious in photos, but always measure the rooms yourself. Take pictures of any damage, because when you leave, the landlord may try to keep part of your deposit to pay for it.
Finally, read the contract. Some landlords don't allow you to decorate or even put pictures on the walls. If you want to save money, consider a flat in the suburbs. The rent is often much lower, and with a few plants and lamps, even a small room can feel cosy.

In many of the world's major cities, housing has become dramatically less affordable. In Bangkok, the average price of a condominium near a train line has risen far faster than salaries over the past decade. For young professionals, getting a mortgage often means committing to thirty years of payments, and many simply cannot qualify.
As a result, more people are living in cramped flats or renting rooms in shared houses. Others are moving further out, to residential areas on the edge of the city, and accepting long journeys to work. Some buy older properties to renovate, hoping to save money, only to discover that the cost of maintenance, from repairing roofs to improving insulation, is far higher than expected.
Older generations face different pressures. Many retired couples are choosing to downsize, selling family homes that are now too large and too full of clutter collected over forty years. In some cities, rising rents have even led to tenants being evicted so that landlords can sell or redevelop the property.
Governments have tried various solutions, from building public housing to taxing empty homes. However, economists warn that there is no quick fix: as long as cities offer the best jobs, demand for housing in them will remain high.
